items.title: Electric Lit’s Top 10 Short Story Collections of 2026
items.summary: It’s been a particularly fruitful year for the short story. In Recommended Reading alone, we’ve had the honor of publishing excerpts from many of our favorite collections of the year. Along with surprising variance and singularity, there are also recurrences across these collections: identity, artifice, and distance—both temporal and physical—mediate the relationships at the core of these books. In her introduction to Lim Sunwoo’s story “That Unfamiliar Night,” translator Chi-Young Kim writes: “Lim beautifully portrays how grounding it can be when someone sees you, when someone is quietly there for you.” Across these collections, a reader has this sense of bearing witness—and being seen—by so many small moments. In Bret Anthony Johnston’s “Paradeability” , a father accompanies his son to a clown convention in Texas; the costumes and air of performance both amplify and conceal vulnerability. In Sydney Rende’s “Monsters” , the dissolution of a relationship is distorted in the funhouse mirror of reality TV. In “Going Up” from Chris Vanjonack’s Out of Body , an anonymous speaker targets a woman plagued by uncertainty. Above all, our favorite collections this year play with ambiguity: What can be revealed when a story withholds a tidy answer to its central questions? This year’s best works of short stories include five debut collections, as well as new collections from veterans of the form, such as Bret Anthony Johnston and Emily Ruskovich. Regardless of where you start, there are many delights to be found above—and below—the surface of these narratives. –Lennie Roeber-Tsiongas Assistant Editor Editor’s note: The following books were hand-selected by Electric Literature staff and interns, with the help of our community of contributors, readers, and friends of the organization. Books by current staff or board members are not eligible for consideration. The 10 titles below are presented alphabetically by title; they are not ranked. All This Want (and I Can’t Get None ) by T Clark Set in a small working-class neighborhood just on the edge of the bustle of New York City, T Clark’s stories are aware of the in-between. All of the Black girls, women, and nonbinary protagonists at the heart of these stories are in-between youth and adulthood, being and becoming, desire and realization. They face unexpected encounters with strangers, try to get just one more glimpse of an ex, get into viral fights, and attempt to simply exist authentically while caught in the riptide of a hypersexualized, patriarchal society. Everything is hungry, piercing, and alive; Clark writes with an awareness of the dynamics at play, even when the characters aren’t. –Rachel Maybee , Editorial Intern Encounters with Unexpected Animals by Bret Anthony Johnston Under the light of the blazing Texas sun, Johnston reveals the ties that bind us to one another. His greatest strength lies in his characters, who are in turns strange, troubled, and deeply relatable; they represent the beating heart of each story. Some of the unexpected animals we encounter are: a baby alligator a father hopes will protect his family, a dog that sets a teenage boy up to discover a closely guarded secret, and a powerful, inspiring herd of wild horses. No matter which page you turn to in this collection, you’ll find an excavation of how relationships form, break, or ultimately endure. Read an excerpt from the collection here. –Rachel Maybee , Editorial Intern Day Care by Nora Lange Nora Lange’s debut story collection left me restless and, quite counterintuitively, eager to stay in that feeling. These are stories of women with children and partners, and without them; they brim with the listless quality of not quite being where one is meant to be, or having what one wants to have. Accompanying this is a wild desire—unfulfilled but unfettered, roving for fulfillment. One story exists inside a snow globe. Another circles a landfill, a summer rental, and a child who’s learning to play the games that words make possible. A third—featuring the unforgettable line, “‘I hope you find the sex you’re looking for’ her mother said, and meant it.”—tracks a single new mother determined to find an outlet for her libido. Perhaps the most restless quality, though, is Lange’s language. A single sentence has the capacity to estrange and create intimacy, to toggle across distances and create a bewildering sense of both motion and stasis. These are stories I’ve returned to more than once this year, and certainly will next year. Read Lange’s interview about the book in EL’s digital pages with legendary author, and her former teacher, Carole Maso. – Willem Marx , Associate Editor Fat Swim by Emma Copley Eisenberg In Fat Swim , the luminous interconnected debut short story collection by Emma Copley Eisenberg, the question of what it means to have a body, and to fully live in that body—to consume, to desire, to be seen and hated and loved and touched—is brought to the fore. Fatphobia is front and center in places, sure, but the embodiment of these characters is the much more powerful takeaway. Their humanity is centered. In the title story, Alice, a lonely, fat, eight-year-old girl living in West Philadelphia, with evolving feelings about her body, becomes friends with a group of fat women who swim at a nearby public pool. “Fat Swim,” “Beauty,” and “Lanternfly,” are three standouts among a collection of truly spectacular short fiction. – Denne Michele Norris , Executive Director and Publisher I Could Be Famous by Sydney Rende In I Could Be Famous , Sydney Rende captures the feverish, modern itch of wanting to be perceived in a culture where visibility is treated as salvation. Set against the sun-baked, synthetic shimmer of Los Angeles, these linked stories track women orbiting the perimeter of relevance: a struggling actress going method in a hot tub showroom, an assistant filming celebrity mansions who develops a taste for petty theft, and strangers tethered to the downward spiral of a former teen heartthrob. What makes Rende’s debut so thrilling is how she balances biting, acidic wit with the genuine ache beneath all the self-invention. Beyond seemingly chasing vanity, her characters are terrified of remaining ordinary. Rende exposes modern fame for what it really is: a hollow secular religion, and an absurd, heartbreaking bid to prove we exist. Read more about this collection in our interview with the author. – Shandela Contreras , Editorial Intern The Memory Museum by M Lin In his introduction to M Lin’s story “Yulan” in Recommended Reading , Jeremy Tiang writes: “If you can make yourself at home anywhere, how do you know where you belong?” This question weaves through the nine stories of The Memory Museum, exploring the relationship between migration, time, and memory. In “Yulan,” a Chinese artist based in Seattle returns to Beijing, where she is confronted with the emotional and physical distance that has emerged between herself and the life that once belonged to her. Other stories reckon with political constraints, censorship, and parenthood; in “Tough Egg,” an artist navigates the government restrictions on her artistic practice; “Scenes From Childhood” imagines a recent past from a distant future. Across these stories, the voice that emerges is both attentive and unflinching, honest and willing to linger in the lived reality of existing between worlds. –Lennie Roeber-Tsiongas , Assistant Editor Nightjar by Emily Ruskovich When I attempt to describe Emily Ruskovich’s Nightjar , I end up orbiting around words like grounded and otherwordly —words that are accurate but inadequate and, of course, evoke completely opposite ideas. In the collection’s title story , 12-year-old Tess discovers magic in the pasture of her family’s rural farm. In any other narrative, magic would look and feel . . . well, magical. items.title: A Night at the 77th National Book Awards
items.summary: The National Book Awards is arguably the year’s biggest night in books. It’s glam (Black-tie! Tuxedos! Champagne!), it’s fun (think cocktails on the dance floor next to literary all-stars), and, at its best, it’s political. It’s a moment for writers to take the stage and speak out against global injustice and the injustices we are facing from within our own industry. Last night’s ceremony was all of the above, and I got to experience it live, reporting the event with former Electric Lit intern Amulya Tadimety, who graciously helped me record the evening. (Shout out to Amulya, who even swapped phones with me so I could write down quotes while she took pictures using the higher-quality camera.) This year featured a phenomenal set of finalists in all categories, many of whom Electric Lit is lucky to have featured in our digital pages. In Fiction, we featured an interview with Valeria Luiselli and a joint conversation with Morgan Thomas and Julián Delgado Lopera , the two trans novelists nominated for the award—an exciting and much-deserved first that I hope marks many more to come. In Nonfiction, we published interviews with Abdelrahman ElGendy , Sara Nović , and Camonghne Felix , as well as a reading list from Joseph Osmundson , who also helped us put together an article about Bret Stephens’ hideous New York Times hit piece about the diversity of the year’s longlist. The event was hosted by Kyle MacLachlan, whose opening remarks set the tone for the night: at times, lighthearted, balanced with appropriate seriousness. He gave a much appreciated nod to library cards and referenced his love of Dune (MacLachlan’s appearance in the David Lynch adaptation was his break-out role). He also said he was confused about why the NBA wanted him to speak at their event, until he realized it wasn’t, well, that NBA, a joke sure to land with anyone who (like me) makes the annual mistake of googling “NBA finalists” when the shortlist drops. MacLachlan also touched on a topic at the top of everyone’s mind, saying that while AI didn’t write his speech—that would be immoral—he was taking all the credit from the human who did, a more industry-accepted course of action. It was a lighthearted way to enter into the AI conversation, a hot topic, and for good reason. Many of the night’s speeches included rallying cries to reject the encroachment of AI on art, an admonishment implicitly directed at the publishing houses in the room (though perhaps meant less for the editors in attendance than for their boss’ boss’ boss). There were even references to outlets doing away with much-needed books coverage (from Kiran Desai, whose mother, Anita, once reviewed Salman Rushdie, the recipient of this year’s Medal for Distinguished Contribution to American Letters, in the now discontinued Washington Post books section). Interestingly, there was no mention of Catapult’s closure, however—a notable silence on a night full of adamant reminders about the importance of keeping literature alive. Initially, I planned to introduce the winners and their statements one by one, but I would be remiss not to acknowledge up front that nonfiction winner Abdelrahman ElGendy was prevented from entering the country to attend the awards ceremony. His absence was acutely felt, an unignorable reminder of the violence of borders and the violence perpetuated by the current Administration. And, as if state-sanctioned harassment weren’t enough, ElGendy’s eligibility for the award was also questioned by The New York Times , before his win, and again afterward , despite the National Book Foundation issuing a statement affirming his eligibility . ElGendy’s absence was also acknowledged by the first winners of the night, David Levithan and Gabriel Duckels, who won the category of Young People’s Literature for their book The Fight of Our Lives . Levithan opened his statement by saying, “We stand in solidarity with any author who is kept from being here tonight.” Each of the night’s winners gave beautiful, moving speeches. Duckels and Levithan, whose book is a history of the AIDS crisis in America, also spoke about the censorship of queer stories. “The past, present, and future of HIV and AIDS cannot be erased,” said Duckels. Levithan gave a powerful statement on the ongoing erasure of trans and queer stories, saying, “Yes, there are people who want to erase our stories from the shelves, but know there are far, far, far more people who want our stories to be heard . . . We will not allow our youth, particularly our trans and nonbinary youth, to go unsupported. We will not let the noise of others drown out the music of who we are.” Centroeuropa , a novel about a widower who uncovers the bodies of dead soldiers while digging up a field he intends to farm on, by Vicente Luis Mora, translated by Rahul Bery, won in Translated Literature. In his speech, Mora addressed the pain of ongoing war and his dream that one day countries standing for peace and protection for all people will be more than the stuff of fiction. Bery cheekily addressed AI in his speech about the art of translation. Referencing an extremely specific element of Centroeuropa that he was tasked with recreating (the book doubles its page count for each chapter, down to the exact word), he said, “In a year where everyone’s talking about AI and its threat to all kinds of human creativity and endeavor, I like to think that, for now at least, this is something the computers couldn’t do.” I was personally thrilled when Brenda Hillman, the poetry winner for Still House in the Desert , directly addressed the press in the room. “We’re grateful for you,” she said, looking at the press tables in the back where us journalists and magazine editors were gathered, “but you know, sometimes poetry gets kind of a short shrift . . . we ask the press to consider [that] best books include poetry too.” I felt immense pride sitting there, knowing that one day later, Electric Lit was publishing our annual list of our favorite poetry collections , a tradition I hope other outlets will adopt. When ElGendy’s Huna won in nonfiction, the award was accepted on his behalf by his editor, Helen Thomaides. She read from a speech written by ElGendy himself, which began with a statement that if we were hearing his words, it meant that he’d achieved a lifelong dream, only to not be able to be in the room for the moment. It made his already towering absence even larger. Thomaides also gave her own speech, speaking of how ElGendy’s “commitment to speaking out against injustice put a target on his back,” and how, after having found refuge in America, he was once again forced to flee. “Now,” she said, “he’s not able to return even as a celebrated visitor.” The final winner, Hannah Lillith Assadi, won in Fiction with Paradiso 17 . Assadi shared that during the course of writing the book, she “experienced deep personal grief and unimaginable collective grief,” referencing cancer’s attack on her father, and the genocide waged against his people. She spoke of the pain woven with beauty in the novel, saying: “Perhaps this is the Palestinian story on this earth. So beautiful, so painful. And isn’t this story all of ours?” It was a fitting way to end the evening. The post A Night at the 77th National Book Awards appeared first on Electric Literature .

items.title: A Call to Action from Electric Literature
items.summary: Dear Reader, Last year, Electric Literature decided not to apply for funding from the National Endowment of the Arts. You might remember that our decision resulted from an Executive Order handed down by the Trump Administration and new compliance guidelines drafted by the NEA, both stipulating that applicants must not “promote gender ideology.” It was a blatant attack on trans people, period—and applying would have been a betrayal of the values held so closely by EL and its community. I was part of the decision to forgo funding, and while it was nerve-wracking to walk away from money we relied on, standing up for our beliefs was a no-brainer. We trusted that our community would have our back and fill the gap. And it did. When I was preparing to take over as Executive Director and Publisher earlier this year, EL had the chance to speak publicly (in an amicus brief attached to a lawsuit targeting the NEA) about how the loss of NEA funding impacted our ability to practice free speech as an independent literary magazine. As I was interviewed by lawyers from the National Coalition Against Censorship, I took a moment to reflect on the prior year. I felt more sure of our decision than ever. Though our funding had been cut, though we had been forced to revise our financial strategy without notice, we stood with the communities whose rights, protection, and humanity we are forever committed to uplifting—trans people and the queer community, people of color, people with disability, immigrants, women. Rather than feeling fearful about what the future might hold, I only felt immense pride. Over the course of this year, I’ve become acutely aware that independence is our greatest asset—which means community is our greatest resource. Because Electric Lit is completely independent, we retain the freedom to defy a government that sometimes wishes to silence us. That independence also means we rely on our people to keep us going. We need to raise $60,000 by the end of the year to ensure we remain a beacon for the writers and stories we most care about publishing. Electric Lit is committed to safeguarding the freedom, dignity, and humanity inherent to creative expression, but we are only as powerful as the people standing with us. An anonymous donor has kicked off our campaign this year with a matching gift of $15,000. Helping us match that gift will get us halfway towards our goal. I believe in Electric Lit, but more than that, I believe in the people that power Electric Lit. Join us in this fight by making a gift today . With warmth and gratitude, Denne Michele Norris Executive Director and Publisher The post A Call to Action from Electric Literature appeared first on Electric Literature .

items.title: Ask Ethan: Do polonium radiohalos support a young Earth?
items.summary: One of the most beautiful things about science is that if even one single piece of robust evidence comes along that contradicts even our most deeply held ideas about reality, it means that our current way of thinking about things must be revised. The observations of Mercury’s orbit in the late 1800s led to the overthrow of Newtonian gravity; the observation that energy was quantized into discrete entities led to the birth of quantum physics; the observation of ultra-faint, variable stars in Andromeda led to the discovery of extragalactic objects and, soon after, to the expanding Universe. Wherever a seemingly contradictory observation occurs, there’s a chance for advancing our best scientific picture of how the Universe works. We have to take immense care to make sure we don’t fool ourselves, but that applies in both directions. We have to make sure we don’t fool ourselves when it comes to accepting the established picture, but we must also make sure we don’t fool ourselves by believing flawed evidence that claims to undermine it. How is one to know what’s going on when different people who claim to be experts make inconsistent, contradictory assertions? That’s what Bob Brown wants to know, writing in to ask: “I received this article — ‘Polonium Radiohalos: Strong Evidence Against Millions of Years’ — from a friend… I’m at a loss as to how anyone should explain to him how this scenario just isn’t possible. Any insights you can provide will be greatly appreciated.” One of the hallmarks of the scientific enterprise is to be able to consider an idea, even an “out there” alternative idea, and subject it to rigorous scrutiny. If it holds up, it cannot be discarded, no matter how absurd it sounds. However, if it crumbles beneath the weight of evidence, it cannot be viable. Let’s take a good look at what’s going on with this new claim. The Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary layer is very distinct in sedimentary rock, but it’s the thin layer of ash, and its elemental composition (especially its severe iridium enhancement), that teaches us about the extraterrestrial origin of the impactor that caused the mass extinction event, enabling us to conclude that it was a carbonaceous asteroid of likely either the CM or CR type. Earth has hundreds of meters worth of sedimentary rock covering its surface practically everywhere, with limestone making up about 10% of the sedimentary rock in total. Credit : James van Gundy The conventional view of planet Earth is that it is, indeed, approximately 4.5 billion years old. The Sun and the Solar System itself is slightly older, while the Earth-Moon system was formed by a collision between two large protoplanets: a proto-Earth and a Mars-sized body named Theia. While many lines of evidence support an old Earth, including: various layers of sedimentary rock with older metamorphic rock beneath them, a fossil record dating back more than 3 billion years, and our knowledge of solar physics, indicating the lifetime of the Sun, the strongest evidence comes from radiometric dating : the measurements of elements and isotopes that arise from the radioactive decay of precursor elements that were present initially on our world. By their very nature, minerals contain a wide variety of elements and isotopes: some of which are stable and others of which aren’t stable, with the unstable ones instead undergoing radioactive decay. Those decays often proceed in a chain: continuing until a final, stable product is reached. If you can know the initial concentration of the (parent) decaying element, the half-life of every element in the decay chain, and can measure the concentration of the (daughter) end product, you can calculate the age of the rock. Those are a lot of “ifs,” of course, but we’ve done that for Earth and for many other bodies in the Solar System, obtaining ages for Earth rocks in the billions of years and for several meteorites of around 4.55-4.56 billion years. That’s the conventional view. This animated version shows the lead isotope isochron that Clair Patterson first used to determine the age of the Solar System and of Earth back in 1956. The animation further shows progressive growth over 4550 million years of the lead isotope ratios within meteorites; the relationship between the lead 207-204 vs. lead 206-204 is key. Credit : Jmpalin/Wikimedia Commons However, there’s a new assertion out by Jake Hebert , claiming that the conventional age of billions of years for the Earth is wrong, and that even millions of years is too long. Instead, he claims that radioisotope dating supports an age that’s just thousands of years old for the Earth: an age that’s consistent with the claims of biblical creationism . This specific claim is that one should look at rocks known as Phanerozoic granites, and at features — or inclusions — within them known as polonium radiohalos. While Hebert notes that the conventional picture claims that these radiohaloes are typically under 541 million years old and that nuclear decay rates (like the laws of physics) are a constant over time, he instead puts forth the idea that the decay rates were accelerated a few thousand years ago, and that the radiohalos from decaying polonium survive as the evidence of that. To understand what he’s claiming, let’s go through what he states, but let’s do it in a way that compares what he’s asserting against the conventional story told by geologists, geophysicists, and nuclear physicists to see where there’s agreement and when there’s something he’s suggesting that’s outside of the realm of what’s generally accepted. New Zealand’s Split Apple Rock is composed of granite, and dates back to the Cretaceous period more than 65 million years ago. The cause of the split down the rock’s center was a naturally occurring joint, and was likely broken apart by a combination of rains and ocean waves. Granite is generally a product of magma or lava that has cooled, and often naturally contains fractures where minerals, veins, or inclusions frequently appear. Credit : Rosino/flickr First, Hebert talks about granites in general (and Phanerozoic granites in particular) as having formed like any igneous rock: when hot magma cools and solidifies. He notes that zirconium silicate crystals often form within these granites, and that sometimes there’s a chemical substitution of (radioactive) uranium for zircon in these crystals. This part is generally true. Granite is a common igneous rock, and it’s generally formed when magma comes to Earth’s surface and erupts (becoming lava, but that’s not an important detail), flows over the land, and cools, becoming solid rock. During the time that the rock is in the liquid state — as magma or lava — any radioactive decays that occur will produce daughter particles that don’t remain; alpha particles (or helium nuclei) become gas and escape, while only the ultimately stable daughter particle persists. It’s for this reason that measuring things like the uranium-to-lead ratio (or the potassium-to-argon ratio, among other radioactive tracers) allows you to date how long it’s been since a rock has formed: since it solidified. The part about this being a Phanerozoic granite just means that it comes from the geological Phanerozoic period : approximately dating from the beginning of the Cambrian period and extending to the present time. Therefore, by definition, it covers the time period of the past 539 million years or so, and Phanerozoic granites represent rocks formed during this time period. So far, this is in full agreement with what’s presently understood. items.title: The black hole information paradox
items.summary: In 1915, an astronomer stationed on the Russian front was supposed to be calculating artillery trajectories. Instead, Karl Schwarzschild solved Einstein’s new equations of general relativity before Einstein himself could, and in doing so he uncovered the math of black holes, objects Einstein spent decades insisting could not exist. Physicist Brian Greene, author of The Elegant Universe and Until the End of Time, uses black holes as a sledgehammer to test what we really know about reality. This video The black hole information paradox is featured on Big Think .

items.title: Why everyone should be doing therapy
items.summary: I would bet my house that you’re living with something. There is some sickness, pain, or condition you’ve learned to deal with. Because there is no such thing as “perfect” health. Everyone you talk to, everyone you see on the street, everyone in the line at the coffee shop, has something they have to adapt to. It might be something mild, like dry skin in the winter or being nearsighted. It might be a chronically bad back or intermittent migraines. Or, it might be something that requires more of us: diabetes tests, dialysis, the latest cancer treatment. Everyone, everywhere, is dealing with something. Mental health is no different. I’m sometimes asked if I’m an anxious or obsessive person, and my reply is almost always the same. Yes, I can certainly feel anxious, and yes, I can display obsessive behaviors, but am I anxious or obsessive? I don’t think so. I am the way I am, and I have learned how to live with that. We all grow to deal with the world as best we can. I have strategies, tools, and ways of thinking that allow me to operate in the world, and I’m sure you do as well. The question, then, is what tools we can call upon. The French philosopher Georges Canguilhem once argued that we shouldn’t necessarily define “health” as perfect function or as a “no boxes checked” on a health questionnaire. Instead, we should define health in terms of a “margin of tolerance” to the world’s misfortunes. To be healthy is to have hard times, experience pain, and endure mental distress, but to get back up again and to get back to living. “Health” doesn’t mean having nothing wrong with you — it’s when you have the power to live with your something. As any good therapist will tell you, therapy is not limited to the hour you are in the room. It’s a method. It’s a way of thinking. This is a new, members-only newsletter all about how to live well. It’s about the strategies that can help us cure or endure what makes us anxious, lost, or unhappy. It’s about the tools and habits that we can call upon to enjoy the richness of life all the more. This newsletter is about how to be healthy in mind and happy in soul. The first edition — coming this Sunday — will be free to all, and after that, it will be bundled into our membership package , where you can get all of our newsletters, articles, and videos. There, you can also register to join online events with the likes of Carlo Rovelli, Alex O’Connor, and Brené Brown. And, of course, US customers can get our quarterly print magazine for free. Why “The Sunday Epicurean”? Over 2,000 years ago in Athens, a man living with his own “something” started a school. Epicurus had a great bushy beard and a lifetime of digestive issues, and he founded “The Garden” — one of the four big schools of antiquity. In The Garden, students weren’t bothered with abstract mathematics or metaphysics. They spent their days talking about human suffering and human happiness. Their curriculum focused on the natural sciences and what we now call psychology. The Friends of Epicurus, as they were called, were encouraged to have regular, introspective therapy sessions. They’d eat together, walk together, and philosophize together. Because, as Epicurus put it, in the same way that medicine is pointless if it does not cure the diseases of the body, there is no point in philosophy if it does not cure the suffering of the mind. I strongly believe that everyone should be doing therapy. But I define “therapy” in a looser, wider sense. On the one hand, we live in an age of therapy. More and more people go to see psychotherapists and psychiatrists. We’re all much more willing to speak in the language of therapy, and many of us are better at reflecting on our inner lives. As a philosopher and an empirically minded sort, I think these are good trends. Therapy works for a lot of people. But, as any good therapist will tell you, therapy is not limited to the hour you are in the room. It’s a method. It’s a way of thinking. It’s a reorientation of your life that allows you to live better. Limiting “therapy” to once a week leaves us poorer. Medicalizing therapy — pathologizing it — makes it forever curative and reactive. Good therapy is what we keep with us. When Epicureans talk about therapy, they mean it in a broader, lived sense. It’s something we do every day. It’s something we do with all of our friends as much as possible and not just with Dr. Carver at 3 p.m. on Tuesdays. In The Garden, Epicurus told his students to introspect often, to take control of their decisions, and to nurture their relationships. He said we should commit to who we are, what we enjoy, and where we are right now. I think he’s right. It’s why I’ve written an entire book about it, called The Art of Enough . So, The Sunday Epicurean is a kind of philosophical therapy. It’s a weekly heart-to-heart conversation where we explore — together — what might be causing us pain and how we might alleviate it. It’s a sit-down meal with Friends in The Garden where we learn about the ins and outs of human psychology and how we can all enjoy more of life. The Sunday Epicurean is a newsletter about how to avoid pain and find pleasure. These newsletters will give a little of me and invite a little from you. I hope you can join our Garden community. I hope you can share strategies, habits, and insights as much as I can. Because, as the Friends themselves knew, we are all in this together. We all suffer, and we all laugh. We all get lonely, and we all love. We all have to work out how to live with our “something.” So let’s work out how to live well, together. This is an edition of The Sunday Epicurean , a weekly, members-only newsletter from Mini Philosophy. This article Why everyone should be doing therapy is featured on Big Think .
